locations.

Hierarchy / flow
(email value)        (row pointer) -------------------------------------- alice@example.com    → row ID 3 bob@example.com      → row ID 7 charlie@example.com  → row ID 10 You can think of it like a mini, specialized table that: Has the indexed column(s) Plus a pointer to where that row lives in the actual table (called the row ID or row reference) 🔍 Example ⚙ Internal Implementation – Data Structures Most relational DBs (like MySQL, Postgres, Oracle) use:
✅ B+ Tree Index (default for most cases) Balanced tree structure Fast lookup (O(log n) time) Sorted, which helps in range queries (>, <, BETWEEN) 🧠 Summary Index is a separate data structure (usually a B+ Tree) — not a table, but like a lookup map. If only one column is indexed, other conditions are still checked row-by-row after filtering. You can improve performance with composite indexes. Use EXPLAIN to analyze query plans and tuning. ================================== 🔹 1. In MySQL (with InnoDB): The Table is also a B+ Tree Wait... what? 😮 Yes! In MySQL’s default engine (InnoDB): ✅ The entire table is stored as a clustered B+ Tree, ordered by the primary key. 📘 What is a "clustered" table? The table rows are the leaf nodes of the primary key's B+ Tree index. So the actual data is inside the B-Tree, and there's no separate table structure! You can think of it like: The table IS the primary index (clustered), and other indexes just point to it.

🔷 Databases & Scaling Concepts (Topics 11–20)

============================ 11. ✅ SQL vs NoSQL ============================ SQL (Structured Query Language): Uses tables with rows and columns Schema is fixed Great for relational data (like banking, inventory)
16.2 SQL vs NoSQL, indexing & database strategies 
Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle NoSQL (Not Only SQL): Flexible schemas, document-based, key-value, etc. Used in high-speed, scalable apps Great for unstructured or hierarchical data Examples: MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis 󰞵 Java + Spring Boot often uses both (via JPA for SQL and Spring Data MongoDB for NoSQL). ============================ 12. 📈 Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) ============================ Add more power (CPU, RAM, SSD) to a single server. ✅ Pros: Simple No code changes ❌ Cons: There's a hardware limit Downtime needed to upgrade ============================ 13. 🌐 Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) ============================ Add more machines (servers or nodes) to handle traffic. ✅ Pros: No limits (in theory) Fault tolerance ❌ Cons: Complex to manage (needs load balancers, sync) Cloud systems like AWS/Azure make horizontal scaling easy with auto-scaling groups. ============================ 14. ⚖ Load Balancer ============================ A system that distributes incoming requests across multiple backend servers. Prevents overloading one machine Increases availability
Common load balancers: NGINX, HAProxy, AWS ELB Think of it like a traffic cop guiding requests to the least busy lane. ============================ 15. 🔍 Database Indexing ============================ An index is like a table of contents for a database — it helps quickly locate rows without

scanning

the

entire

table.

Speeds up SELECT queries But slows down INSERT/UPDATE a bit Needs careful design for performance Use indexes on columns often used in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY. ============================ 16. 🔁 Replication ============================ Creating copies of your database to improve: Read performance Fault tolerance (if master fails, read replicas still work) Types: Master-Slave (writes go to master, reads can go to replicas) Multi-Master (writes possible on multiple nodes – complex) ============================ 17. 🧩 Sharding ============================ Split one big database into smaller parts (shards), often by: User ID range Geography Some hash Each shard holds a subset of the data. Like breaking up a giant spreadsheet into smaller ones so different teams can handle each

chunk.

============================ 18. 🧱 Vertical Partitioning ============================

Splitting a single table into multiple smaller tables based on columns. Why? Reduce I/O by only reading what’s needed Improve cache performance Example: Users Table (ID, Name, Email, Photo, Bio)  ↓ Users_Core (ID, Name, Email)   Users_Profile (ID, Photo, Bio) ============================ 19. ⚡ Caching ============================ Store frequently-used data in memory (RAM) to serve faster. Reduces database load Increases speed dramatically Common caches: Redis Memcached Think of caching like bookmarking a frequently visited page so you don’t search every time. ============================ 20. 🔄 Denormalization ============================ The opposite of normalization. You intentionally duplicate data to reduce JOINs and improve read speed. Faster reads, especially for reporting But harder to maintain consistency Use in read-heavy systems like dashboards, analytics, etc.
17 Scaling & Reverse Proxy
17.1 Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling

horizontal vs Vertical Scaling

📈 1. Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) ✅ What It Means: You increase the resources of a single machine — more CPU, RAM, SSD, etc. 🧠 Analogy: You replace your laptop with a more powerful one to handle more Chrome tabs. 🛠 How It’s Done: Upgrade physical server: add more RAM, better CPU Use cloud instance resizing (e.g., switch from t2.micro to t2.large in AWS) For databases: upgrade to a more powerful managed instance (e.g., RDS upgrade) ✅ Pros: Simple to implement No need to change application architecture Often cheaper short-term ❌ Cons: Hardware limit: There’s only so much RAM/CPU you can add

Visual reference — original diagram / table

Single point of failure: If this one powerful server crashes, everything’s down Scaling up = downtime (reboot/redeploy) ============================= 🌐 2. Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) ✅ What It Means: You add more machines (instances/nodes) to handle the load, instead of making one machine

stronger.

🧠 Analogy: Instead of upgrading your one laptop, you hire 5 assistants, each doing part of the job. 🛠 How It’s Done: Spin up multiple servers running the same app Put a load balancer (like NGINX, AWS ELB) in front of them Backend services often run as stateless microservices to support this Common in Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, EC2 Auto Scaling 💻 In Java Apps: You deploy multiple instances of your Spring Boot app, like: Instance 1 → 10.0.0.1:8080 Instance 2 → 10.0.0.2:8080 Instance 3 → 10.0.0.3:8080 And place a reverse proxy/load balancer in front. ✅ Pros: Infinite scaling potential High availability (if one instance dies, others still run) No need to shut down for upgrades ❌ Cons: More complex setup (load balancers, service discovery) Shared data/storage becomes a challenge Requires stateless design (or external session store) 🔐 When to Use Each
Use Vertical Scaling when: You’re just starting out You need a quick performance boost You have a monolithic app Your app is stateful and not yet ready for distribution =========== Use Horizontal Scaling when: You have high traffic or expect growth Your system is stateless or microservices-based You want zero downtime scaling You’re in the cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure) ----------------------------------- =========== 󰳕 In Practice with Java + Spring Boot =========== Scenario Scaling Strategy 1. Your app runs slow on EC2- Try vertical scaling first 2. Load spikes crash your single node- Add a load balancer and horizontal scale 3. Microservices with many users-- Always go horizontal 4. High latency DB queries-  Vertical scale DB first

🔒 Reverse Proxy – Security Explained

🔒 Reverse Proxy – Security Explained When we say "security" in the context of a reverse proxy, we’re mostly talking about: 1. Hiding the Backend Servers Clients only see the reverse proxy (e.g., myapp.com), not internal IPs or ports (like 10.0.0.5:8080). This makes it harder for attackers to target specific app servers directly. 2. Rate Limiting & DDoS Protection Reverse proxies can limit how many requests per second are allowed from each IP. Helps prevent abuse or basic DDoS attacks (spamming your app).
17.2 Reverse proxy, load balancing, security & geo controls 
3. IP Whitelisting / Blacklisting You can allow or deny specific IP ranges at the proxy level. Example: Only allow internal IPs to access admin pages. 4. Basic Authentication / Header Checks Reverse proxies can require username/password for certain paths. Can inspect headers to block suspicious requests (e.g., bots). 5. Firewall Rules Acts as a first line of defense before requests reach your app logic.

What is a Reverse Proxy?

🔁 What is a Reverse Proxy? A reverse proxy is a server that sits in front of one or more backend application servers. It receives incoming client requests, and forwards them to the appropriate internal server. Clients think they’re talking to one server, but behind the scenes there could be many. 🔧 Core Functions of a Reverse Proxy Routing : purpose is to route client request to correct handler. Load Balancing: seems to control trafic of request SSL termination: responsible to entry https request. Caching : holds frequest sue data ================= 1. Routing ================= The reverse proxy inspects the URL path and decides which internal service should handle the

request.

Hierarchy / flow
/api → sent to the backend API service /auth → sent to the authentication service / → sent to the frontend web server This is very useful in microservices architectures.

================= 2. Load Balancing ================= When you have multiple servers handling the same service, the reverse proxy can split traffic

between

them.

This: Prevents any one server from being overloaded Helps scale your app to handle more users Adds high availability (if one server crashes, others still handle traffic) ================= 3. SSL Termination ================= SSL (HTTPS) encryption/decryption is CPU heavy. The reverse proxy can handle all HTTPS connections from the client, then forward requests to

the

internal

app

servers

over

HTTP.

This: Keeps your backend simple (no SSL setup on each app server) Centralizes HTTPS logic (easier to manage certificates) ================= 4. Caching ================= A reverse proxy can store copies of frequently accessed content, like: Static files (images, CSS, JS) API responses that don’t change often (e.g., blog list) When the same request comes again, the proxy responds immediately, without bothering the

backend.

This: Reduces load on your app servers Speeds up response time for users ================= 5. Security  ================= The reverse proxy improves security in several ways:
Hides internal architecture (IP, ports, paths) Blocks or limits abusive traffic (rate limiting) Filters requests by headers or IP (access control) Acts as an entry point firewall Can require authentication for sensitive paths ==================================== 🛠 How to Implement Reverse Proxy ===================================== Common tools used: NGINX – lightweight, super popular HAProxy – high-performance load balancer Apache HTTP Server – with proxy modules Cloudflare – SaaS reverse proxy + CDN AWS ALB – managed reverse proxy in cloud ===================================== You configure them to: ======================================= Listen on port 80/443 Route to backend services running on other ports or servers Handle HTTPS, headers, rate limits, etc.

Forward Proxy with example

🌍 1. Geo-Unblocking & VPN – France DB Example ✅ Your understanding: Correct! Let’s say your Java app connects to a production database hosted in France, and only IPs from

France

are

allowed

(for

security).

🔒 If you’re in India, your request is blocked. ✅ Solution: Connect via VPN (France) or use a French forward proxy, so your traffic appears to come from

France. Now the French DB sees: Request from: 185.23.98.101 (A French IP) → ✅ Allowed This is geo-network trust enforcement — often used in: Data regulations (GDPR) Private APIs or databases Country-based rate limiting ================================ 🚫 2. Filtering – Facebook Block Example ====================== ✅ Your understanding: Spot on again! Let’s say your proxy is configured by the company to block Facebook. Even if your browser requests: https://www.facebook.com The forward proxy sees it and says: ❌ "Access Denied: Facebook is blocked." So you get an error page. 🔐 Who sets this up? Companies, Schools, Libraries Managed by network administrators via proxy rules ======================== 👀 3. Monitoring – Is My Gmail Being Watched? ================================== 👁 What they can see depends on HTTPS and the proxy’s power. Case Can Proxy See? What It Can See You visit HTTP site ✅ Full content, page data, everything You visit HTTPS site 🚫 (partially) Only the domain name, not your actual content 🔒 So what about Gmail or LinkedIn? These sites use HTTPS (SSL encrypted). The proxy can see you're visiting mail.google.com or linkedin.com, but not: Your email text Chat messages

Login credentials ✅ Unless... If the company uses SSL interception proxy (like ZScaler), then: 🔓 They can decrypt your HTTPS traffic using their own root certificate, inspect it, and then

re-encrypt

it.

You'll usually be warned about this when using corporate laptops (custom certs installed). =================== 🧪 4. Testing – What does that mean? ================== Here’s what it means in simple terms: As a developer, you might want to: ✅ Simulate a user from different locations (e.g., US vs Germany) ✅ Test how your API behaves with slow or blocked connections ✅ Check if geo-restricted APIs or services work properly ✅ Emulate a mobile app calling via different IPs 💡 Example: You’re building a weather app, and: US users get Fahrenheit EU users get Celsius You can test this by routing your request through forward proxies from those countries.

Proxy: an intermediate server (Foward vs Reverse)

🔁 What is a Proxy? A proxy is an intermediate server that sits between a client and another server, forwarding

requests

and

responses.

Hierarchy / flow
🟢 1. Forward Proxy Used by the client to communicate with the internet while hiding the client’s identity. ✅ How it works: [Client] → [Forward Proxy] → [Internet Server]
🔍 Purpose: Hide client IP Control internet access Bypass geo-restrictions Add filtering or monitoring 🛠 Common Use Cases: 1. Anonymity / Privacy Hide real client IP address 3. Parental / Company Filters Block specific content or domains 5. Geo-Unblocking Appear as if you're in another country 7. Monitoring Log traffic for analysis or policy 🧪 Tools / Providers: Squid Proxy (open source) Privoxy (privacy-focused) Commercial VPNs (also use proxy tech) Proxy providers: Bright Data (Luminati) Smartproxy Oxylabs import java.net.*; public class ProxyExample {     public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {         // Proxy configuration         Proxy proxy = new Proxy(Proxy.Type.HTTP, new InetSocketAddress("proxy.example.com", 8080));         // Target URL         URL url = new URL("http://example.com/api/data");         HttpURLConnection conn = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection(proxy);         conn.setRequestMethod("GET");
int responseCode = conn.getResponseCode();         System.out.println("Response Code: " + responseCode);     } } ====================== 🟡 2. Reverse Proxy ====================== Used by the server to control and route traffic to backend systems while hiding them from the

client.

Hierarchy / flow
✅ How it works: [Client] → [Reverse Proxy] → [Internal Servers] 🔍 Purpose: Load balancing SSL termination (handle HTTPS encryption) Caching static content Security/firewall Routing to microservices 🛠 Common Use Cases: Use Case Description Load Balancing Distribute traffic across servers SSL Termination Offload SSL work from backend servers Caching Cache static assets (CSS, images, etc.) Microservice Routing Route based on URL path (e.g., /api) DDoS Protection Block suspicious clients early ⚙ Popular Tools: NGINX (very common, easy config) HAProxy (high-performance) Apache HTTP Server Cloudflare (SaaS reverse proxy + CDN) AWS ALB (Application Load Balancer)
18 Top 30 System Design Concepts
18.1 Client-server, DNS, proxy, HTTP/HTTPS, APIs & GraphQL

30 Design Principles concept

🟩 1. Client-Server Architecture =========================== 📘 What it is: A model where the client requests data/services and the server provides them. 🧠 Analogy: Think of a restaurant: You (client) order food (request). The kitchen (server) prepares it and sends it back (response). 💻 In tech: Browser = client Website backend = server Browser (Client)  --->  HTTP Request  ---> Server                     <--- HTTP Response <--- =========================== 🟩 2. IP Address =========================== 📘 What it is: An Internet Protocol address is a unique number assigned to every device on a network. 🧠 Analogy: Think of it like a home address for your computer — so others know where to send data. 📦 Example: 192.168.1.1 (IPv4) 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 (IPv6) =========================== 🟩 3. DNS (Domain Name System) =========================== 📘 What it is:
DNS translates human-readable domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses. 🧠 Analogy: Like a phonebook for the internet. You type youtube.com, DNS tells your browser it’s at 142.250.64.238. =========================== 🟩 4. Proxy / Reverse Proxy =========================== 📘 What it is: A proxy is a middleman between a client and a server. Proxy (Forward Proxy): Sits between client and server to hide the client. Reverse Proxy: Sits in front of servers to hide/scale the servers. 💡 Use cases: Caching Load balancing Security Client --> Proxy --> Server    ← Forward Proxy Client --> Reverse Proxy --> Backend Servers  ← Reverse Proxy =========================== 🟩 5. Latency =========================== 📘 What it is: Time delay between a request and the response. 🧠 Analogy: Like the pause after you ring someone’s doorbell before they answer. Low latency = fast response High latency = slow, laggy 💡 Measured in milliseconds (ms) =========================== 🟩 6. HTTP / HTTPS ===========================

📘 What it is: HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol HTTPS = Secure version (encrypted with SSL/TLS) 💡 Used to transfer web data (HTML, JSON, etc.) http://example.com → Not secure https://example.com → Encrypted and secure =========================== 🟩 7. APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) =========================== 📘 What it is: Set of rules that let software talk to each other. 🧠 Analogy: A waiter in a restaurant. You (client) talk to the kitchen (server) only via the waiter (API). APIs │ ├── REST API (Most Common) ├── SOAP API ├── GraphQL API └── gRPC (Modern) =========================== 🟩 8. REST API =========================== 📘 What it is: A type of API that follows REST (Representational State Transfer) principles, using HTTP. 💡 Uses methods like: GET – retrieve data POST – create data PUT – update data DELETE – delete data =========================== 🟩 9. GraphQL ===========================

📘 What it is: A newer API style where clients specify exactly what data they need, unlike REST. 🧠 Analogy: REST is like ordering a fixed meal. GraphQL is like a customizable buffet – get only what you

want.

{   user {     name     email   } } =========================== 🟩 10. Databases =========================== 📘 What it is: Structured systems to store and retrieve data. Types: SQL (Relational): Tables, schemas (e.g., MySQL, PostgreSQL) NoSQL: Flexible, document-based (e.g., MongoDB) ============================ 11. ✅ SQL vs NoSQL ============================ SQL (Structured Query Language): Uses tables with rows and columns Schema is fixed Great for relational data (like banking, inventory) Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle NoSQL (Not Only SQL): Flexible schemas, document-based, key-value, etc. Used in high-speed, scalable apps Great for unstructured or hierarchical data Examples: MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis
18.2 SQL/NoSQL, scaling, indexing, replication, sharding, caching & advanced concepts 
󰞵 Java + Spring Boot often uses both (via JPA for SQL and Spring Data MongoDB  for NoSQL). ============================ 12. 📈 Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) ============================ Add more power (CPU, RAM, SSD) to a single server. ✅ Pros: Simple No code changes ❌ Cons: There's a hardware limit Downtime needed to upgrade ============================ 13. 🌐 Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) ============================ Add more machines (servers or nodes) to handle traffic. ✅ Pros: No limits (in theory) Fault tolerance ❌ Cons: Complex to manage (needs load balancers, sync) Cloud systems like AWS/Azure make horizontal scaling easy with auto-scaling groups. ============================ 14. ⚖ Load Balancer ============================ A system that distributes incoming requests across multiple backend servers. Prevents overloading one machine Increases availability Common load balancers : NGINX, HAProxy, AWS ELB Think of it like a traffic cop guiding requests to the least busy lane.
15: Indexing ============================ 15. 🔍 Database Indexing ============================ Index: usually B+Tree Index node: contains id + pointer to row An index is like a table of contents for a database — it helps quickly locate rows without

scanning

the

entire

table.

Speeds up SELECT queries But slows down INSERT/UPDATE a bit Needs careful design for performance Use indexes on columns often used in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY. ============================ 16. 🔁 Replication ============================ Creating copies of your database to improve: Read performance Fault tolerance (if master fails, read replicas still work) Types: Master-Slave (writes go to master, reads can go to replicas) Multi-Master (writes possible on multiple nodes – complex) ============================ 17. 🧩 Sharding ============================ Split one big database into smaller parts (shards), often by: User ID range Geography Some hash Each shard holds a subset of the data. Like breaking up a giant spreadsheet into smaller ones so different teams can handle each
chunk. ============================ 18. 🧱 Vertical Partitioning ============================ Splitting a single table into multiple smaller tables based on columns. Why? Reduce I/O by only reading what’s needed Improve cache performance Example: Users Table (ID, Name, Email, Photo, Bio)  ↓ Users_Core (ID, Name, Email)   Users_Profile (ID, Photo, Bio) ============================ 19. ⚡ Caching ============================ Store frequently-used data in memory (RAM) to serve faster. Reduces database load Increases speed dramatically Common caches: Redis Memcached Think of caching like bookmarking a frequently visited page so you don’t search every time. ============================ 20. 🔄 Denormalization ============================ The opposite of normalization. You intentionally duplicate data to reduce JOINs and improve read speed. Faster reads, especially for reporting But harder to maintain consistency Use in read-heavy systems like dashboards, analytics, etc.

Hierarchy / flow
- 5 design principles in oops programming. - intended to make software designs more understandable, flexible, and maintainable. Software Design Principles │ ├── SOLID Principles (5 OOP Design Principles) │   ├── S - Single Responsibility Principle │   ├── O - Open/Closed Principle │   ├── L - Liskov Substitution Principle │   ├── I - Interface Segregation Principle │   └── D - Dependency Inversion Principle │ └── General Software Development Best Practices      ├── DRY - Don't Repeat Yourself      ├── KISS - Keep It Simple      ├── YAGNI - You Aren't Gonna Need It
19.2 SOLID principles
Hierarchy / flow
├── Separation of Concerns (SoC)      ├── Composition over Inheritance      └── Law of Demeter ===================== S - one Class one Role O- Extend class, Methods L- Object replacement(Liskov Substitution Principle) I- Specific Interface(create smaller interface) D- Independent Modules(higher class module should not dependent on lower module- use

abstraction)

=================== 1. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP):(class) One class should have only one reason to change. -class should have only one responsibility or job. Example: A User class should handle user data storage, but not email notifications. 2. Open/Closed Principle (OCP):(class, methods) -Reuse existing code. -you should be able to extend the behavior of a module without modifying its source code. Example: Instead of modifying PaymentProcessor, create a new CreditCardPaymentProcessor
class.

3. Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP):(Objects) -objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without affecting

any

desirable

properties

of

the

program

or

the

correctness

of

the

program.

- Liskov Substitution Principle states that a subclass should be able to replace its parent class

without

changing

the

correctness

or

expected

behavior

of

the

application.

If

replacing

the

parent

with

the

child

causes

unexpected

behavior,

then

inheritance

is

incorrect

and

LSP

is

violated.

-  Example: A Rectangle should be substitutable for a Square.  i.e if we pass 1 side, and square reference, then it may calculate square area. but if we pass 2 side, rectangle may be calculated.

If B IS-A A, then object of B should replace object of A without changing program behavior. 4. Interface Segregation Principle (ISP):(specific interface) -segregation-separationg - creating smaller, more specific interfaces rather than large, general-purpose ones Example: Separate AuthenticationInterface from UserManagementInterface. 5. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP):(Modules) - High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. -both should depend on abstractions. Example: Inject DatabaseConnection interface into a service class instead of directly

instantiating

a

database

connection

object.

=============================== 2 ⃣ Detailed Explanation + Java Examples 🧱 DRY – Don’t Repeat Yourself 🔹 Meaning: Every piece of knowledge or logic should have a single, unambiguous representation in your

codebase.

❌ Bad Example (Violation): // Two different methods calculating tax separately double calculateTaxForInvoice(double amount) {     return amount * 0.18; } double calculateTaxForProduct(double amount) {     return amount * 0.18; } ✅ Good Example (DRY Applied): private static final double TAX_RATE = 0.18; double calculateTax(double amount) {
19.3 DRY, KISS & YAGNI 
return amount * TAX_RATE; } Now, if tax rules change, you update it once , and all usages stay consistent. 💡 In Spring: Reuse services instead of duplicating logic in controllers. Example: Common OrderService used by both web and API layers. 🧱 KISS – Keep It Simple, Stupid 🔹 Meaning: The simplest working solution is usually the best one. ❌ Bad Example (Overengineering): public String getHello() {     return Optional.ofNullable("Hello").map(String::toUpperCase)         .filter(s -> s.length() > 0)         .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Empty!")); } ✅ Good Example (Simple & Clear): public String getHello() {     return "HELLO"; } 💡 KISS in Practice: Don’t build generic frameworks for problems that don’t exist yet. Avoid excessive abstraction layers unless you have clear reuse needs. Simplicity reduces bugs and onboarding time for new developers. 🧱 YAGNI – You Aren’t Gonna Need It 🔹 Meaning: Don’t add functionality until it’s actually required by the business or system. ❌ Bad Example: // Adding complex discount system even though business doesn’t need it yet if (user.isPremium()) {     applyLoyaltyDiscount();
} else {     applySeasonalDiscount(); } ✅ Good Example: // Build for today’s actual need applyStandardDiscount(); 💡 YAGNI in Practice: Avoid speculative “future-proofing.” Every line of code has a maintenance cost. Build iteratively — add when it’s justified by a user story or metric.

20.2 Static vs Singleton & Java class hierarchy

static vs singleton

A static nested class cannot be a top-level class, but static nested class CAN implement

interfaces

.

A static nested class can have both instance and static members. Static nested class is initialized when it is first actively used (as part of Java class loading rules). Singleton can be: Eager Initialization Lazy Initialization Double Checked Locking Bill Pugh Singleton A static class object is stored in stack whereas singlton class object is stored in heap memory

space.

Java Classes │ ├── Language Features │   │ │   ├── final class │   ├── abstract class │   ├── static nested class │   └── inner classes │ └── Design Patterns      │      └── Singleton Class

Factory Method Pattern( creates objects based on input (like a

string

or

enum):

hide

object

creation

logic)

The Factory pattern provides a centralized class (a factory) that creates objects based on input

(like

a

string

or

enum),

without

exposing

the

exact

class

being

instantiated.

You call the factory to get an object, and the factory decides which class to return. =============================== e. g.  interface ElectricityPlan{} Class domestic implements ElectricityPlan{} Class Commercial implements ElectricityPlan{} ============================= 🧠 Why Use the Factory Pattern? 1. To centralize object creation logic. 2. To avoid using new keyword scattered across your code. 3. To make it easier to introduce new types without changing existing code. 4. To return subclasses based on runtime input or configuration. 5. To follow Open/Closed Principle — open for extension, closed for modification.
21 Factory, Prototype, Singleton & Abstract Factory — Detailed Examples
21.1 Factory Method — motivation, implementation, benefits & usage 
============== Now Factory class creates instance as per requirement/data. Advantage: • Factory Method Pattern allows the sub-classes to choose the type of objects to create. • It promotes the loose-coupling. Usage of Factory Design Pattern • When a class doesn't know what sub-classes will be required to create • When a class wants that its sub-classes specify the objects to be created. • When the parent classes choose the creation of objects to its sub-classes. ================================== 💡 Real-World Examples 1 UI Component Factories In frameworks, you often call something like ButtonFactory.createButton("windows") or "Mac". 2 Document Generators You might have DocumentFactory.create("pdf") or "word" and it returns the appropriate

document

class.

3 Database Driver Selection Based on config: DatabaseFactory.getConnection("mysql") or "postgresql". 4 SAP Reports or Forms A factory decides which report format to generate based on input (e.g., PDF, SmartForm,

Excel).

5 Spring Framework Spring internally uses factory-like mechanisms to instantiate beans (BeanFactory, FactoryBean). ============================= ❌ Without Factory (Tightly Coupled Code) Shape shape = new Circle(); // hard-coded

- Now your main code knows about Circle, Square, etc. - If you change the class name or logic, you’ll break many places. ✅ With Factory (Loosely Coupled Code) Shape shape = factory.getShape("circle"); // main code doesn’t care how it's built You can change how objects are created without touching client code. You can switch between implementations at runtime. ======================================= 🧠 When to Use It (Summary) You have a superclass/interface and many subclasses You want to decide object creation at runtime You want to follow SOLID principles (especially OCP and SRP) You need a way to hide object creation logic ======================

Prototype Design Pattern(template based: using clone())

Here we clone existing objects instead of creating new ones from scratch (using new), which

can

be

expensive

or

complex.

It provides a copy mechanism using the clone() method, often implemented via the Cloneable

interface

in

Java.

e.g Form filling is a great real-world example of the Prototype pattern. or creating a report on tool from existing template.

Visual reference — original diagram / table
21.2 Prototype — cloning, shallow/deep copy, benefits & use cases 
🧠 Pattern-wise: The template form is the prototype object. Each filled form is a clone of the prototype, modified for a specific user. =========================== Advantage of Prototype Pattern o It reduces the need of sub-classing. o It hides complexities of creating objects. o The clients can get new objects without knowing which type of object it will be. o It lets you add or remove objects at runtime.  Usage of Prototype Pattern • When the classes are instantiated at runtime. • When the cost of creating an object is expensive or complicated. • When you want to keep the number of classes in an application minimum. ✅ Summary Feature Prototype Pattern Purpose Clone existing objects instead of creating new ones Benefit Performance, memory efficiency, flexibility Java Mechanism Cloneable + clone() Cloning Type Shallow (default) or Deep (manual) Use Case Games, UIs, object templates, configuration 🚨 The Problem: Expensive or Repetitive Object Creation Sometimes, creating a new object using new is: ============================== 💡 Real-Life Examples In a drawing app: You create a circle, set its color and size, and then clone it to create similar

shapes.

In a game: You create one enemy prototype, then spawn 100 clones with different positions. In a reporting tool: You have a base report layout that you clone and customize for different

In an object pool: Instead of reinitializing everything, you clone a clean template object. In SAP: You define a base SmartForm or configuration and clone it for multiple versions.

# Singleton: creational design patterns | Serialiazation | Clone

Class is defined in such a way that only one instance of the class is created through the JVM e.g. Cache, Logger, Configuration File, Runtime Class, Desktop class 🚨 Why Do We Need Singleton? 1. You don’t want multiple Loggers writing to different log files. since each logger will try to

create

its

file.

2. You don’t want two caches holding separate copies of data. 3. You don’t want conflicting settings/configs from multiple config instances. ✅ Solution: Singleton Use the Singleton pattern to create one central, shared instance that is: Lazily loaded Thread-safe (if needed)

Abstract Factory Pattern(Create multiple related objects

together)

Create multiple related objects together =========================== 🔥 Problem Statement Imagine you’re building a GUI application or SAP-based UI, and you want to support multiple UI

themes:

• Windows theme

21.4 Abstract Factory — UI themes, document families & SAP examples

• Mac theme • Dark mode • Light mode Each theme must provide a set of UI components: • Button • Checkbox • Dropdown • TextField Now you want to switch the theme dynamically — and make sure that when one theme is

active,

all

components

match

(e.g.,

no

Mac

checkbox

in

a

Windows

layout).

✅ Why Do We Need Abstract Factory? The Factory Pattern helps when you need to create a single object — like a Button or Shape. But what if you need to: • Create multiple related objects together (Button + Checkbox + Dropdown) • Ensure those objects are compatible (e.g., all are part of the Windows family) That’s where Abstract Factory shines. It creates entire families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes. 🧠 When to Use Abstract Factory 1. You need to create families of related objects (e.g., different UI kits, device drivers, database

connectors).

2. You want to ensure objects are used together consistently. 3. You want to switch product families at runtime (e.g., from Windows to Mac UI). 4. You want to follow the Open/Closed Principle — easily add new families without modifying

existing

code.

💡 Real-World Examples 1. Cross-platform GUI toolkit Each OS (Windows, Mac, Linux) has different Button, Checkbox, etc. 2. Database Drivers A database factory returns different implementations for MySQL, Oracle, or PostgreSQL

connections.

3. Document generators

One factory creates PDF header + footer + body; another creates Word-style header + footer +

body.
